title: Web Performance Optimization
tagline: Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP), bundling and code-splitting, lazy loading, HTTP caching strategies, CDN architecture, and the practical techniques that make pages fast.

sections.content:
Web performance is not an afterthought — it directly impacts user retention, conversion rates, and search rankings. Google's **Core Web Vitals** are user-centric metrics that quantify real-world experience: how fast does the main content appear (LCP), does the layout shift unexpectedly (CLS), and how quickly does the page respond to interactions (INP).

But fast pages are not achieved by a single trick. They require a layered approach: delivering less code (bundling, tree-shaking, code-splitting), deferring non-critical code (lazy loading), reusing prior responses (caching), and delivering assets from geographically close servers (CDN). This topic covers the full toolkit — from Lighthouse scores to deployment strategies.

sections.caption: Web performance optimization falls into four strategies: reduce total work, defer non-critical work, reuse previous results, and distribute delivery geographically.

sections.title: Web Performance as a Restaurant
sections.content:
Think of a web page as a restaurant meal:

- **LCP** is when the main course arrives — the most important content visible to the user.
- **CLS** is a clumsy waiter rearranging your table items as you reach for them — unexpected layout shifts are jarring.
- **INP** is how quickly the waiter responds when you wave for attention — interaction latency.

Optimization strategies map to restaurant improvements:
- **Bundling/minification** is using smaller serving dishes (less to carry, faster to deliver).
- **Code splitting** is serving courses progressively — appetizer first, main when ready — instead of carrying everything at once.
- **CDN** is opening restaurant branches near customers — less distance to travel.
- **HTTP caching** is pre-preparing dishes for repeat customers: 'I know you always order the same thing'.
- **Lazy loading** is not preparing the dessert menu until someone asks — why carry it if most people leave early?

**Core Web Vitals**: - **LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)**: When does the largest visible element (hero image, `

`, large `

`) render? Target: under 2.5 seconds. Common causes of slow LCP: render-blocking resources, slow server (high TTFB), large unoptimized images. - **CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)**: Sum of all unexpected layout shifts while the page loads. A score of 0 is perfect; under 0.1 is 'Good'. Caused by: images without explicit `width`/`height`, ads/embeds injecting content, web fonts causing FOUT, dynamically injected content above existing content. - **INP (Interaction to Next Paint)**: Measures the latency of ALL user interactions (clicks, taps, key presses) and reports the worst. Replaces FID. Target: under 200ms. Caused by: long tasks on the main thread, expensive event handlers, non-yielding JavaScript. **Bundling and Tree-shaking**: Module bundlers (Vite, webpack, esbuild) combine many JS files into fewer bundles. **Tree-shaking** (dead code elimination) removes exports that are never imported. Ensure you import only what you use: `import { debounce } from 'lodash-es'` not `import _ from 'lodash'` (which includes all 600+ utilities). **Code Splitting**: Split your bundle into chunks loaded on demand. Route-based splitting loads only the code for the current page. Component-level splitting loads heavy components only when rendered. Dynamic import (`import()`) is the mechanism. **Lazy Loading**: Images and iframes below the fold can use `loading="lazy"` — the browser skips downloading them until they are near the viewport. JavaScript components can use dynamic `import()` to load only when needed. **CDN (Content Delivery Network)**: A CDN places cached copies of your static assets at edge servers worldwide. A user in Tokyo gets assets from a Tokyo edge server rather than your US-based origin. This reduces latency from network round trips and reduces load on your origin. CDNs also handle DDoS mitigation, TLS termination, and HTTP/2 push.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: `PerformanceObserver` lets you measure Core Web Vitals in the browser without external libraries. LCP fires multiple times — the last entry is the actual LCP. CLS must exclude entries with `hadRecentInput` (user-triggered scrolls/zooms don't count). Dynamic `import()` is the core mechanism for code splitting — the bundler will create a separate chunk file that is only downloaded when the import executes.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: The three Core Web Vitals each target a different aspect of user experience: loading (LCP), visual stability (CLS), and interactivity (INP). Fixing LCP usually means optimizing the critical rendering path and image delivery. Fixing CLS requires explicit sizing of all media. Fixing INP requires breaking up long tasks and optimizing event handlers.

sections.content: **Start with measurement, not guessing**. Run Lighthouse (Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse tab) on your page to get a scored report with specific recommendations. Use **PageSpeed Insights** (pagespeed.web.dev) for field data from real Chrome users (Core Web Vitals from the CrUX dataset). The three highest-ROI improvements for most apps: (1) set `width` and `height` on images to eliminate CLS, (2) add `fetchpriority="high"` to the LCP image to improve LCP, and (3) code-split your bundle so the initial JavaScript payload matches only what the current route needs.

items: **Core Web Vitals** — LCP (<2.5s), CLS (<0.1), INP (<200ms) — are Google's user-centric performance metrics that directly affect search ranking and user experience.
**Code splitting** with dynamic `import()` prevents loading JavaScript for routes or features the user has not visited. Bundlers automatically create separate chunk files per dynamic import.
**Tree-shaking** eliminates unused exports at build time. Use named imports from ES module packages (`import { x } from 'lib'`) to enable it — default imports often pull in entire libraries.

**Images cause both LCP and CLS problems**: use `fetchpriority="high"` on the hero image (LCP), set explicit `width`/`height` attributes on all images (CLS), use `loading="lazy"` for below-fold images, and serve WebP/AVIF formats.
**CDNs** reduce latency by serving assets from geographically close edge servers. Pair with content-hashed filenames and `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable` for zero-latency repeat visits.

quiz.question: What does LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) measure?
options: The time for the very first pixel to appear on screen
When the largest visible content element (image or text block) has rendered
The time until the page becomes fully interactive
The total number of layout shifts during page load
quiz.explanation: LCP measures when the largest visible content element — typically a hero image, H1 heading, or large text block — finishes rendering. Good LCP is under 2.5s from navigation start. It represents when the main content is visible, which correlates with perceived page load speed. FCP (First Contentful Paint) measures the first pixel; TTI measures interactivity.

quiz.question: Which attribute on `` tags prevents Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)?
options: loading="lazy"
decoding="async"
Explicit width and height attributes
fetchpriority="low"
quiz.explanation: Setting explicit width and height attributes tells the browser the image's aspect ratio before it loads, so it reserves the correct space in the layout. Without them, the browser allocates zero space initially, then shifts the layout when the image loads — causing CLS. Modern CSS aspect-ratio can also achieve this.

quiz.question: What is tree-shaking in the context of JavaScript bundlers?
options: Removing unused CSS selectors from stylesheets
Eliminating JavaScript code (exports) that is never imported or used
Splitting a large bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand
Compressing JavaScript with Brotli or gzip
quiz.explanation: Tree-shaking is dead code elimination at the module level — if you import { debounce } from 'lodash-es', the bundler can detect that all other lodash functions are unused and exclude them. It requires ES modules (import/export) since CommonJS (require) is dynamic and cannot be statically analyzed.

quiz.question: What does `import('./chart.js')` (dynamic import) enable?
options: It runs the module in a Web Worker
It loads the module synchronously at parse time
It splits chart.js into a separate bundle chunk loaded on demand
It imports only specific named exports from chart.js
quiz.explanation: Dynamic import() returns a Promise and is the code-splitting point for bundlers like Vite and webpack. The bundler creates a separate chunk file for the dynamically imported module, which is only downloaded when import() is called at runtime. This keeps initial bundle size small — the chart code is only fetched when the user needs it.

quiz.question: What does `` do?
options: Decodes the image on a background thread
Defers loading the image until it is near the viewport, reducing initial page weight
Uses a lower resolution placeholder until the full image downloads
Marks the image as non-critical for LCP measurement
quiz.explanation: loading=lazy defers downloading images that are below or near the viewport fold. The browser only fetches them as the user scrolls toward them. This reduces initial page weight and speeds up LCP (fewer bytes competing for bandwidth). Do NOT use lazy on the LCP image — it delays the most important content.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of a CDN (Content Delivery Network)?
options: Compressing JavaScript bundles at build time
Caching and serving static assets from geographically close edge servers to reduce latency
Providing DDoS protection through traffic analysis
Splitting JavaScript bundles into smaller chunks
quiz.explanation: A CDN's primary purpose is geographic distribution — placing cached copies of assets at edge servers near users worldwide. A user in Tokyo gets assets from a Tokyo edge server instead of a US origin, dramatically reducing network round-trip time. CDNs also reduce origin load, improve availability, and often provide TLS termination and DDoS mitigation as secondary benefits.

quiz.question: INP (Interaction to Next Paint) replaced which previous Core Web Vital?
options: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)
FID (First Input Delay)
TBT (Total Blocking Time)
quiz.explanation: INP replaced FID (First Input Delay) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. FID only measured the delay of the very first user interaction. INP measures the worst-case latency across ALL interactions during the page lifetime, providing a more complete picture of responsiveness. Both measure interaction latency but INP is more comprehensive.

quiz.question: To make a content-hashed JavaScript bundle (`app.a1b2c3.js`) optimally cached, what Cache-Control header should the server return?
options: no-store
no-cache
max-age=3600, public
max-age=31536000, immutable
quiz.explanation: Content-hashed assets have unique URLs that change when the content changes. They should be cached for as long as possible (1 year = 31536000s) with immutable to tell browsers to never revalidate. When you deploy a new version, the hash changes, creating a new URL — old cached files are simply never requested again.

quiz.question: Which `` attribute tells the browser to prioritize downloading the LCP image?
options: importance="high"
fetchpriority="high"
preload="true"
loading="eager"
quiz.explanation: fetchpriority="high" signals to the browser that this resource should be fetched with high priority. On the LCP image, this ensures the browser starts downloading it as soon as it is discovered in HTML, rather than waiting for lower-priority resources. It is more targeted than preloading and works directly on the element.

quiz.question: A user imports `import _ from 'lodash'` in their app. What problem does this cause?
options: lodash is incompatible with modern bundlers
The entire lodash library is included in the bundle, even if only debounce is used
Default imports cause circular dependency errors
The import will fail unless lodash is also imported via a CDN link
quiz.explanation: Importing the entire lodash default export brings all 600+ utilities into the bundle. Bundlers cannot tree-shake CommonJS modules effectively. The fix: use lodash-es (ES module version) with named imports: `import { debounce } from 'lodash-es'`. The bundler then only includes debounce. This can reduce bundle size by 500KB+ for lodash alone.
